newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Commerce chief cites progress with China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Commerce chief cites progress with China.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said on Saturday that the best way for the Clinton administration to make progress with China on trade and human rights issues was to keep expanding contacts with the Asian giant.

"The fact is we're moving the ball forward," Kantor insisted during an interview on CNN's "Evans and Novak" programme less than a week after U.S. President Bill Clinton's meeting in the Philippines with Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
Kantor, who is leaving the administration to return to private life, rejected the suggestion that Clinton had ignored civil rights issues in his talks with Jiang in favour of trade.
"You cannot move the ball forward on human rights or on non-proliferation or on relations in Asia, or stability and peace or economics, without full and complete engagement," Kantor said.
Clinton met the Chinese leader on the fringes of a meeting in Manila of the 18-country Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

Kantor said there was no doubt that China discriminates against U.S. products and services, with the United States running up huge monthly deficits in trade that now surpass the U.S. shortfalls with Japan. He said the Chinese discrimination must end.

"We have fought very hard to get rid of that discrimination through industrial agreements, agreements in agriculture and agreements on intellectual property rights protection in trying to get China to adhere to the commercially reasonable agreement to get into the World Trade Organisation," Kantor said.
"We're making some progress, but we have not solved the problem," he added.
Aides said Clinton told Jiang a week ago that he looked forward to China joining the WTO, which regulates world trade.
But China was told it must offer freer market access.

Washington has blocked China's bid to enter on easier terms granted to underdeveloped countries. Chinese officials said the two presidents agreed "a pragmatic and flexible attitude" was needed by both sides.

Kantor did not directly respond to questions about the pressure being brought to bear on Walt Disney Co by China. The U.S. entertainment company has been warned it should stop making a movie about the Dalai Lama if it wants to maintain its access to Chinese markets.
It was "Disney's choice to make" on the issue, Kantor said. The United States must balance economic and political interests and pursue "thoughtful diplomacy," he added.
